title: The regular integer model at the generic prime
statement: Let $\iota:\mathbf Q\to L$ be a finite purely inseparable field extension [def-weil-pbc-finite-purely-inseparable-extension], and let $B=\operatorname{im}(\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Q\xrightarrow{\iota}L)$, with its induced $\mathbf Z$-algebra structure. Then $\iota$ is surjective and the map $\mathbf Z\to B$ is a ring isomorphism. The ring $B$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] and regular [def-weil-regular-scheme]: for every prime ideal $\mathfrak q$ of $B$, its localization $B_{\mathfrak q}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is regular local. Moreover, $B$ is finite as a $\mathbf Z$-module, generated by $1$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]; every element of $L$ is $b/c$ for some $b,c\in B$ with $c\ne0$; and $\operatorname{Spec}B$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] is nonempty and is itself a regular open subset.

source.place: Tag 07PJ, proposition-ubiquity-J-2, proof of case (3), verification of condition (4) of lemma-J-2: the zero-prime regular finite model, including the integer prime-local regularity calculation (returned proof Steps 1 and 3).

proof.text: In characteristic $0$, the definition of purely inseparable says that the extension equals its base field. Thus $\iota$ is surjective. It is injective: a nonzero $r\in\mathbf Q$ in its kernel would give $1=\iota(r)\iota(r^{-1})=0$. The composite $\mathbf Z\hookrightarrow\mathbf Q\xrightarrow{\iota}L$ is therefore injective, and its corestriction $e:\mathbf Z\to B$ is a ring isomorphism by the definition of $B$ as its image.

source.place: Tag 09HE, definition-purely-inseparable, final paragraph: the convention in arbitrary characteristic

proof.text: Every $b\in B$ is $e(n)=n\cdot1_B$ for an integer $n$, so $\{1_B\}$ generates $B$ as a $\mathbf Z$-module. For $x\in L$, choose $a/d\in\mathbf Q$ with $d\ne0$ and $\iota(a/d)=x$. Then $x=e(a)/e(d)$ inside $L$, with $e(d)\ne0$ by injectivity. These are the asserted finite-module and fraction clauses.

source.place: Tag 07PJ, proposition-ubiquity-J-2, case (3), generic-prime instance of condition (4) of lemma-J-2

proof.text: The integer-localization node states that $\mathbf Z$ is Noetherian. If $I\subset B$ is an ideal, choose generators $n_1,\ldots,n_r$ of $e^{-1}(I)$. For $b\in I$, write $e^{-1}(b)=\sum_j a_jn_j$; then $b=\sum_j e(a_j)e(n_j)$. Hence $I$ is finitely generated and $B$ is Noetherian.

source.place: Tags 034X (lemma-characterize-Dedekind) and 00FM (section-Noetherian); integer case recorded in lem-weil-pbc-z-localizations-dvr

proof.text: For a prime $\mathfrak q\subset B$, put $P=e^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. It is prime since $e(ab)=e(a)e(b)$. The fraction formulas $a/s\mapsto e(a)/e(s)$ and $b/t\mapsto e^{-1}(b)/e^{-1}(t)$ define inverse ring maps $\mathbf Z_P\simeq B_{\mathfrak q}$: denominators avoid the corresponding prime, and the defining fraction relation is preserved by $e$ and $e^{-1}$. An isomorphism gives inverse bijections on ideals by image and inverse image; these preserve inclusions, prime ideals and generating sets. Consequently they preserve Noetherianity, locality, Krull dimension and the number of generators of the maximal ideal, hence regular locality.

source.place: Tags 00CO (definition-localization), 00KU (definition-regular-local), 00FM (section-Noetherian): explicit fraction and ideal identifications

proof.text: By the integer-localization node, either $P=(0)$ and $\mathbf Z_P\cong\mathbf Q$, or $P=(p)$ for a rational prime $p$. In the first case the field-regularity node gives regular locality. In the second case that same integer-localization node gives a Noetherian local domain of dimension $1$ with maximal ideal generated by $p/1$. This generator is nonzero: $p/1=0$ would mean $up=0$ for an integer $u\notin(p)$, impossible in $\mathbf Z$. Apply the principal-maximal-ideal regularity node. Step 4 now gives regular locality of every $B_{\mathfrak q}$, so $B$ is regular.

source.place: Tag 00PD, lemma-characterize-dvr, conditions (3) and (4); Tag 00KU, definition-regular-local, dimension-zero field case; Tag 00OD, definition-regular

proof.text: The ring $B$ is a nonzero subring of the field $L$, so $(0)$ is a prime ideal: a product vanishes only if one factor vanishes. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}B$ has the point $(0)$. The whole spectrum is open in itself and is an affine open neighbourhood of each of its points, with Noetherian regular coordinate ring $B$ by Steps 3 and 5. The definitions of affine spectrum and regular scheme therefore make it a nonempty regular open subset of itself.

lean.statement: theorem range_generic_regular_model (L : Type u) [Field L] [Algebra ℚ L] [Module.Finite ℚ L] [IsPurelyInseparable ℚ L] : Function.Surjective (algebraMap ℚ L) ∧ Function.Bijective (algebraMap ℤ (Int.castRingHom L).range) ∧ IsNoetherianRing (Int.castRingHom L).range ∧ IsRegularRing (Int.castRingHom L).range ∧ Module.Finite ℤ (Int.castRingHom L).range ∧ Submodule.span ℤ ({1} : Set (Int.castRingHom L).range) = ⊤ ∧ (∀ x : L, ∃ b c : (Int.castRingHom L).range, (c : L) ≠ 0 ∧ x = (b : L) / (c : L)) ∧ Nonempty (AlgebraicGeometry.Spec (CommRingCat.of (Int.castRingHom L).range)) ∧ AlgebraicGeometry.IsRegularScheme (AlgebraicGeometry.Spec (CommRingCat.of (Int.castRingHom L).range))
